answer_md:
🐾 At **Norfolk Southern**, the initial rollout of his team’s engineering practices didn’t stick.

Pair programming, test-first development, and continuous integration had been in place from the start, but the engagement still reached a quality crisis. Developers had resisted the new ways of working, the client was operating in mainframe thinking, and account leadership was accustomed to waterfall. Matt’s account identifies missing reinforcement and follow-up: implementing the practices had not been enough to keep people using them.

The recovery included an audit, a rebuilt backlog, and TDD experts from Columbus pairing side by side with the team to redo the work properly. But those experts were temporary. Then the pandemic removed co-location—the condition the pairing method had been built around.

Matt rebuilt the team’s daily workflow so test cases came before engineering the solution, inside a pair, with progress checked at standup. Pairs rotated daily, and new engineers worked alongside seasoned practitioners. Stories entered sprints only when discrete and testable, with defined scenarios and a definition of done. They were capped at **3 points** to fit a **1-week** iteration. For remote work, pairs traded drivers frequently and pushed and pulled code before each trade.

The practices held after the experts left, and the failure mode that caused the crisis did not recur. Release cycles shortened and delivery became more predictable; the story does not quantify those improvements. Matt’s own lesson was that “implementing a practice is the easy half”—reinforcement, follow-up, and verification had been missing the first time.

answer_md:
🐾 Matt describes his leadership approach as empathy, clarity, and modern engineering rigor.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, teams were designed for autonomy, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. But practitioners arriving from command-and-control organizations sometimes reverted to waiting for direction and sending decisions upward. As the centers scaled to **150+ practitioners**, pockets of fear of blame persisted. Matt had to reinforce the working model repeatedly; the path was bumpy.

He brought product managers, designers, and engineers into cross-functional teams with shared ownership and decision-making authority. Leaders acted as facilitators, and team leads focused on removing obstacles rather than controlling outcomes. Matt made intent explicit, pushed decisions to the people closest to the work, and used direct feedback and open communication. He grounded engineering work in automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices. His leadership-philosophy account reports **4x delivery acceleration** once teams embraced lean product and modern engineering practices.

His “permit to fail” practices included non-punitive post-mortems, low-stakes experiments, and open retrospectives. He shared his own experiences with mistakes and met with team members about their challenges and aspirations. Teams applied lessons to subsequent sprints, reduced recurring failure patterns, and reported improved morale; turnover declined.

With client leadership, Matt used “I do, we do, you do” coaching and **6-week** Agility Coaching Labs on teams’ actual work. He created shared language across business and technology teams and restructured delivery around business domains. Those engagements reported **15–**35%** cost reductions**.

He also made decisions and constraints explicit: governance reviews exposed security tradeoffs, while security-focused engineers embedded checks into delivery. Those engagements achieved **100% compliance** with PCI DSS, GDPR, and SOX. At **RBC**, he presented a data-migration strategy to senior leadership that the client adopted; at **Fiserv**, he brought an accessibility manifesto to IT leadership, the steering committee, and delivery teams, who adopted it as an ongoing development standard.

So there is a concrete example of fragmentation and extra cost during the organization’s growth. There isn’t a documented example here of Matt’s leadership style causing a failed engagement. answer_md:
🐾 At **Norfolk Southern**, the practices Matt introduced didn’t stick at first.

Pair programming, test-first development, and continuous integration had been in place from day one. But developers had resisted the new ways of working, the client was operating in mainframe thinking, and account leadership was accustomed to waterfall. A quality crisis followed. An audit, a rebuilt backlog, and TDD experts from Columbus pairing side by side with the team were needed to redo the work properly.

Matt’s account explicitly identifies what had been missing: reinforcement, follow-up, and verification. Implementing the practices wasn’t enough. The outside experts were temporary, and the pandemic then removed the co-location the method was built around.

Matt rebuilt the team’s day so test cases became a discrete step before engineering the solution, inside a pair, checked at standup. Rather than mandating compliance, he paired newer engineers with seasoned practitioners for “showing, doing, and reaffirming” through repeated iterations. Pairs rotated daily, each pulling a single story from the prioritized backlog. Stories entered sprints only when discrete and testable, with defined scenarios and a definition of done, capped at **3 points** within a **1-week** iteration. For remote work, pairs traded drivers frequently, pushing and pulling code before each trade.

The practices held after the experts left, and the failure mode that caused the crisis did not recur. Matt’s stated lesson was his as much as the team’s: “implementing a practice is the easy half, and reinforcement, follow-up, and verification are what make it real.”

It documents a concrete limitation during scaling and the changes he made in response; I don’t have a documented example here where his approach failed outright.

🐾 Yes—at **Norfolk Southern**, the initial working model wasn’t producing the quality Matt expected.

On the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement, modernizing the Revenue and Shipment Planning platform, Matt brought in a balanced team and emphasized test-driven development. A couple of months in, as the pandemic forced remote work, the client reported rising defects—even though the dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The failure landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership rather than defending the metrics. A bottom-up audit found an engineer solutioning from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete, but defects went undetected. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

The correction went beyond asking engineers to follow the process. Matt showed the gaps openly, rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories, and brought in frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the team. They redid the code and test cases. He introduced Samman-style coaching: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. Product managers also received SMART story training.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Client confidence was restored. The story records an initial failure and a subsequent correction—not an engagement that remained unsuccessful.

🐾 Matt’s payments work includes **JP Morgan Chase**’s ACCESS Next Generation platform and cross-border payment workflow design for **RBC**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, regional payment systems had different formats, protocols, data models, and entitlement structures. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but the bank needed purpose-built payment modules and controls beyond its out-of-box capabilities. Corporate administrators were spending days configuring permissions manually, while live payment operations had to continue through the migration.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase** in the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He designed and delivered ACH credits and direct debits, Fedwire and international wires, FX/cross-border payments, and government tax payments. The FX module connected to the bank’s foreign exchange engine so corporate treasurers could initiate cross-currency payments with embedded rate visibility.

He also delivered the centralized payments gateway: message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**, replacing fragmented point-to-point integrations. Payment controls included Message Authentication Code verification, sanctions screening, and payment-type-specific permissions—for example, allowing wire approval without FX initiation. A new grouping capability let administrators change permissions across users, accounts, and products from a single screen, reducing entitlement management from days to minutes.

Matt led the payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. Migration compliance dashboards became standard operational tooling. ACCESS launched in **April 2011** as a unified corporate banking portal serving **135,000+** clients across **180+ countries**.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems, manual processes, and missing real-time FX tools were delaying cross-border payments. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, working with the FX team on currency conversion and transaction visibility. His design included real-time FX, automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and bulk processing. The deliverable was a complete implementation blueprint—not a claimed platform launch. Revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays and improved SLA compliance.

🐾 Here’s a concrete example of “teaches teams to fish”: Matt’s Enterprise Java course at **American InterContinental University**.

Students came in with no server-side experience. Matt taught the course in late **2003** and early **2004**, alongside a full-time consulting engagement. He had previously built a product in JSP alone, watched it become fragile and slow, and taught himself the MVC pattern to refactor it. For the course, he used the same book—Marty Hall’s *Core Servlets and JavaServer Pages*—and wrote to the author, who sent slides and examples for the class.

Matt structured each phase around an assignment that produced running code, rather than something students only read about. They started by installing the JDK and Apache Tomcat, then built HTML forms, handled requests with servlets, and added MySQL persistence through JDBC. They used a shopping cart to work through session tracking and the stateless nature of HTTP.

He introduced MVC at the end, after students had encountered the problems it addressed: servlets became controllers, JavaBeans and MySQL formed the model, and JSP provided the view. The pattern arrived as an answer to problems they had already hit, rather than an abstraction handed to them upfront.

Students finished with a working Java web application with persistence and session state. **A year later**, a student preparing for his first developer interview contacted Matt to ask what to review.

Across the center, teams achieved **4x** delivery acceleration once they embraced lean product and modern engineering practices—not an outcome attributed to brainstorming alone.

🐾 Here’s the payments work behind ACCESS and **RBC** Express.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt worked on ACCESS Next Generation from **August 2009 to June 2012**. The bank’s regional payment systems had different data models, entitlements, message formats, and compliance requirements. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform supplied the foundation, but its out-of-box capabilities did not cover the needs of **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase**, with engineers in Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He determined where WebSeries configuration ended and bespoke engineering was required, spending **70–80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules—including NACHA file validation, settlement options, and integration with the bank’s foreign exchange engine.

He also built the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and payment routing across **12** countries, replacing fragmented point-to-point integrations. Payment controls included Message Authentication Code verification, sanctions screening, and payment-type-specific permissions—for example, allowing wire approval without FX initiation. For administrators, he replaced individual permission changes with role-based profiles and bulk grouping, reducing entitlement management from **days to minutes**.

Matt led payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. He introduced compliance dashboards, ran production validation, and owned on-call and critical incident response. ACCESS and its Integrated Global Payments Interface launched in **April 2011**.

At **RBC**, from **June 2012 to June 2013**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border payments. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, partnering with the FX team on real-time currency conversion and transaction visibility. His implementation blueprint covered automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and bulk processing. Revised cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays; training materials supported business clients’ independent adoption of multi-currency management. This engagement delivered the design and implementation blueprint—not a claimed production-platform launch.

🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio.

Clients needed to test ideas involving connected devices, voice, computer vision, and robotics before committing budget. Traditional custom hardware/software integration was too slow and expensive—especially when sensors, actuators, and cloud services had never been wired together before. Matt worked on this at the Atlanta Innovation Hub from **November 2019 to September 2023**.

Matt started with the client’s problem rather than a technology demonstration. He used design thinking, journey mapping, and UX/CX pain-point interviews to define what needed solving. He brought the client and the cross-functional **Accenture** team together in tight, iterative feedback loops, moving from whiteboard to validated prototype in hours and days.

The team turned journey maps and friction points into crude visual mocks, validated them with users, then moved through wireframes and prototypes with successive validation loops. For physical devices, they iterated with cardboard, **3D** printing, and laser-cut materials before building working hardware with sensors and actuators. Instead of building bespoke tooling from scratch for each client, Matt used a reusable, purpose-fit prototyping toolkit.

One container-breach demonstration sent a live alert to a visiting client’s own phone. A customized robotic bartender combined AWS Rekognition, IoT Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and Alexa.

The work produced working prototypes across **5** industries and compressed idea-to-prototype timelines from months of custom integration to hours and days of iterative prototyping. Clients could test a working demonstration before making an investment decision.

🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center.

In the center’s early stages, a rigid hierarchical culture made team members slow to share ideas. Ideas weren’t flowing freely, and the team was missing opportunities to improve project timelines and quality. Matt’s task was to change how people worked together—not simply introduce another process or tool.

He established weekly brainstorming sessions where all ideas were considered without judgment. He emphasized the shared mission and de-emphasized individual accolades, focusing the team on collective success. He also recognized people for contributions that advanced project goals, rather than centering recognition on individual achievement.

Those were specific changes to both the team’s conversations and what received recognition: a regular place to contribute ideas, consideration without judgment, and acknowledgment tied to shared project goals. Engineers, designers, and product team members could contribute toward the same mission.

The brainstorming sessions produced solutions that positively affected project timelines and quality. Open communication and shared goals strengthened team cohesion, and the team identified more efficient ways to reach project milestones as ideas began flowing more freely. This particular account does not attach a numerical improvement to those results.

Matt describes his broader leadership practice as pushing decisions to the people closest to the work and coaching teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks.

🐾 Here’s an example from **JP Morgan Chase**.

ACCESS Next Generation had to replace fragmented regional payment systems while real customer payments continued flowing. Connectivity differed across **12 countries**, and local regulations imposed conflicting requirements for data visibility and access. The team also faced aggressive Wall Street delivery timelines; the underlying vendor platform couldn’t meet all the bank’s requirements out of the box.

Matt managed a blended onshore/offshore team of **40+** across the bank and **Accenture**, with engineers in Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He defined the onshore-offshore engagement model and progressively spent **70–80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline Technologies’ Portsmouth offices, coordinating where the vendor platform’s native capabilities ended and custom engineering was needed.

When production issues surfaced, Matt owned on-call and severe-incident response. He coordinated cross-team root-cause analysis with New York, offshore engineers, and the vendor team, while running status updates and daily leadership calls. For a payment-security failure, he used break-glass production access to query live payment data; the investigation traced the problem to missing unit tests and weak error handling.

For the international rollout, he worked with regional compliance officers and engineers to translate regulatory requirements into specific configuration decisions. Instead of a single big-bang global deployment, he sequenced launches by regulatory readiness and introduced verification dashboards before each regional launch.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**. The gateway unified payment connectivity across **12 countries**, and the legacy payment-data migration completed with **zero disruption** to live payment operations.

🐾 Here’s a concrete example of Matt teaching people to build for themselves.

At **American InterContinental University**, Matt taught entry-level students who had no server-side experience. Rather than introduce MVC as an abstraction upfront, Matt structured each phase around an assignment that produced running code. Students started by installing the JDK and standing up Apache Tomcat. Matt wrote to Marty Hall with questions about the material, and the author sent his own slides and examples for the class. Matt closed the course with MVC—servlets as controllers, beans and MySQL as the model, and JSP as the view—after students had encountered the problems the pattern addressed.

Students finished with a working Java web application with persistence and session state. **A year later**, a student preparing for his first developer interview contacted Matt to ask what to review.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how the two engagements compare.

Execution & Delivery ran through both, but the starting problems differed. At **Fiserv**, Matt took over a **\$8.5M** white-label card portal after repeated missed deadlines, poor quality, and threats of contract cancellation. Its **45-person** team and **3** external vendors were also navigating a mainframe-to-API transition. At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS required custom payment capabilities beyond Bottomline’s WebSeries platform, plus consolidation of fragmented regional systems without interrupting live payments.

At **Fiserv**, Matt’s work combined program recovery with changes to the working model. He reset the backlog and timelines, ran daily onshore/offshore transition calls, and coordinated payment-processing, fraud-detection, and hosting dependencies. Rather than continue with SVN conflicts, manual builds, and hotfixes, he introduced Git, mandatory senior-developer reviews, story-linked unit tests, Maven, Artifactory, Hudson CI, and SonarQube/JUnit quality gates within SOX constraints. He also filled the team’s accessibility expertise gap: learning WCAG standards, leading semantic HTML refactoring, defining an accessibility manifesto, and training developers to maintain compliance across branded portals.

On ACCESS, Matt managed a **40+** blended team and spent **70–80%** of his time embedded with Bottomline. The engineering decision was where to configure WebSeries and where bespoke development was required. He delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax-payment capabilities; MAC payment verification; payment-specific entitlements; risk-based approval controls; contextual help; reporting; and SSO. He also designed the gateway’s message transformation and routing across **12 countries**. For migration, he coordinated legacy-data verification, preserved compliance traceability, introduced compliance dashboards, and owned rollout validation and production incident response.

**Fiserv** finished **3% under budget**, met **47 acceptance criteria**, and launched with **zero critical defects**. Recovering a delayed release avoided **\$500K** in penalties; developers subsequently maintained accessibility compliance independently. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**. Its gateway replaced fragmented integrations, and legacy client configurations, entitlements, and transaction histories migrated without disruption to live payment operations.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how the two engagements compare.

Both involved Execution & Delivery and Risk & Responsible Tech, but the starting problems differed. **Fiserv** was a delivery recovery: its **\$8.5M** white-label card portal had missed consecutive deadlines, quality was poor, and stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. **JP Morgan Chase** ACCESS was a global consolidation and custom-engineering program: regional treasury systems had different data models and payment connections, while Bottomline’s WebSeries platform needed capabilities beyond its out-of-box offering.

At **Fiserv**, Matt coordinated **45** team members and **3** external vendors covering payment processing, fraud detection, and hosting. He traveled to Omaha Monday–Thursday, ran **7 AM** and **11 PM** transition calls, reset priorities and timelines, and resolved cross-vendor dependencies. Alongside the mainframe-to-API transition, he replaced SVN with Git, required senior-developer reviews and unit tests, and introduced Maven, Artifactory, Hudson, and SonarQube. With no accessibility expertise on the team, he also became the ADA/AODA subject matter expert, led semantic-markup refactoring across onshore and offshore teams, and trained developers to maintain compliance across client brands.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt managed a **40+** blended **Accenture**/bank team across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He defined the onshore-offshore engagement model and spent **70–80%** of his time embedded with Bottomline in Portsmouth, coordinating where native platform functionality ended and bespoke engineering began. His work covered ACH, wire and FX payment modules, MAC security, payment-specific entitlements, reporting and SSO, plus a gateway connecting payment rails across **12** countries. He coordinated legacy-data verification with compliance teams, introduced compliance dashboards, and ran cross-team incident response and daily leadership calls during production issues.

**Fiserv** delivery stabilized within **3 months**; the program finished **3% under budget**, met **47 of 47** acceptance criteria with **zero critical defects** at launch, and avoided **\$500K** in penalties. Teams independently maintained accessibility compliance. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries; the gateway unified regional payment connections, and legacy migration completed without disruption to live payments.

His work covered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, tax payments, MAC security, payment-specific entitlements, SSO, and reporting. He also delivered gateway connectivity across **12 countries**, coordinated legacy-data verification with compliance teams, and directed production incident response and daily leadership calls. Migration completed without disruption to live payments; compliance dashboards became operational tooling. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a portal serving **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**.
